transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2025-06-15 09:38 PDT
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Evan (CTO CloudWave), Maya (Platform Eng), Liam (Security)

[00:00] Jordan: okay everyone, thanks for carving out time this morning, quick agenda — deep dive on Private VPC networking for Redwood Private, perf targets, and a bench plan. feel free to interrupt.
[00:22] Evan: thanks Jordan, we've got Maya and Liam on to validate feasibility. main ask: lowest possible p95 for a 4k-8k context model while keeping data inside our VPC, and no public egress if possible.
[00:40] Samira: got it. just to set expectations — Private uses PrivateLink-style endpoints plus an NLB in the Redwood-managed account that we expose into your VPC via Interface endpoints, or we can run the control plane in your VPC with direct ENIs for fully private on-prem-style installs. there are tradeoffs for cross-AZ bandwidth and latency.
[01:05] Maya: can you clarify the PrivateLink pattern? we worry about cross-AZ hops and double-bounce where traffic leaves AZ, goes to NLB in another AZ and comes back.
[01:20] Samira: yes, that's common. recommended pattern is per-AZ NLBs with interface endpoints resolved to the AZ-local NLB IPs via endpoint DNS. that keeps path within AZ for most traffic. if endpoints are misconfigured or you have asymmetric routing, you can get hairpinning.
[01:45] Liam: how about NAT? we want zero public egress for inference data — only necessary egress is to ops for metrics and to your private control plane. can that be done without NAT gateways?
[02:05] Samira: you can avoid NAT by using VPC endpoints for all deps (S3 via Gateway endpoints, Secrets Manager, KMS via PrivateLink where supported), and by routing metrics to your internal metrics collector. if Redwood needs to pull model layers or images initially we'd typically pull through a controlled egress or via a customer-provided S3 mirror — avoid public internet path.
[02:30] Evan: okay, so in practice we mirror model artifacts to our S3 and Redwood pulls from there?
[02:38] Samira: yes, that's what larger customers do. we support pulling from presigned URLs inside your VPC; the bootstrap transfer is a one-time cost.
[02:50] Jordan: small note — for dedicated GPU pools we place pods across AZs to increase availability, which can mean some cross-AZ KV cache warms.
[03:05] Maya: speaking of KV cache, we're sensitive to cross-tenant kv leakage and to encryption at rest. what isolation guarantees exist?
[03:18] Samira: good call. KV cache is per-deployment and scoped to the pod/instance. for Private we run isolated tenants on dedicated pools by default if you contract that, otherwise we use software isolation plus namespace-level keys. disk encryption + KMS per-customer is supported.
[03:38] Liam: can you quantify overhead for per-AZ NLBs and extra ENIs? we're tight on IPs in our subnets.
[03:50] Samira: each interface endpoint consumes an ENI and private IP. one endpoint per AZ per service is typical. if you're IP-constrained we can use smaller subnets for endpoints or a centralized proxy pattern but that increases latency. we'll share a sample subnet plan.
[04:12] Evan: latency targets — what p50/p95 does Redwood realistically hit for 4k vs 8k context when hosted inside customer VPC with per-AZ NLBs?
[04:25] Samira: caveat, depends on model size and batch settings. for an optimized 13B quantized model we've seen p50 ~20-30ms token, p95 around 90-140ms token for single-token loops inside same AZ with small batching. for 8k context the KV cache lookups add some overhead — initial long-context cold-start can be several hundred ms while KV warms. for throughput at scale we rely on continuous batching which can amortize per-token.
[05:00] Maya: curious about batching — we want low tail latency for interactive UI but also cost efficiency for background generation. how do you tune batching in private?
[05:12] Samira: we expose batching windows and max-batch-size per route. two patterns: conservative low-latency window (2–5ms) for UI routes and async high-batch window for background jobs. Redwood Optimize can recommend these settings by analyzing your traffic pattern. note: aggressive batching increases p95 but lowers tokens/sec cost.
[05:40] Liam: quantization — does 4-bit/8-bit quant affect cache consistency or deterministic outputs important for auditing?
[05:50] Samira: quantization affects numerical fidelity so tiny differences in output are expected; we track a quality regression suite tied to prompts to detect drift. for strict determinism you can pin CPU (FP32) or higher-bit quant models, but cost goes up. we'll share quantization profiles and eval deltas.
[06:10] Evan: route tables and DNS — we run split-horizon Route53 private hosted zones. how do you recommend mapping privatelink DNS names?
[06:22] Samira: best practice is to create an alias in your private hosted zone that resolves the Redwood service FQDN to the VPC endpoint interface addresses. that way your apps talk to api.redwood.internal (or whatever) and resolve locally. avoid hardcoding IPs. also ensure your resolver is configured to prefer AZ-local endpoint IPs.
[06:46] Jordan: important operational note: health checks on the NLB must be from customer-managed health subnets or allow our health probe CIDRs — otherwise the NLB will mark backends unhealthy and traffic will shift AZ. we'll include the cidr list.
[07:05] Maya: what about cross-account role access for S3/KMS? we prefer not to hand over full KMS access.
[07:16] Samira: we use IAM roles with narrowly scoped STS assume role or customer-managed kms grants. for HSM customers we can integrate via external key wrap; for most, KMS Grant patterns suffice.
[07:30] Evan: perf bench — can you run a realistic bench inside our test VPC? we want to iterate on subnet sizing and NLB placement.
[07:38] Samira: yes, we'll spin a bench harness that provisions ephemeral endpoints in your account or uses our endpoint patterns. we'll need your VPC CIDR, AZs, and a test subnet with free IPs. bench will capture p50/p95/p99 for single-token and streaming multi-token workloads, and measure cold vs warm KV cache.
[07:58] Liam: security — audit logs for inference calls, token-level tracing, and retention windows; how granular are logs and can you route them to our SIEM?
[08:12] Samira: we can stream structured traces to your collector using Kinesis or direct HTTPS to your ingest endpoint. Redwood can redact PII and only emit metadata by request. call-level auditing with request IDs is standard in Private. retention windows are configurable per contract.
[08:30] Jordan: quick intermittent notes — we sometimes see DNS caching on app side cause AZ mismatch; recommend low TTL on endpoint names during rollout.
[08:42] Maya: what about failover — if AZ X loses NLB, do you recommend explicit cross-AZ DNS failover or relying on endpoint IPs?
[08:55] Samira: rely on per-AZ endpoints + health checks. for faster failover you can add a small client-side logic to try the local IP first then fallback; Route53 health checks for interface endpoints are often slow.
[09:12] Evan: any hidden costs? like cross-AZ data transfer for KV cache replication, or NLB hourly charges?
[09:22] Samira: call those out — NLB hourly + per-GB, ENI IPs, cross-AZ data transfer for traffic between AZs, and NAT cost if you use NAT gateways. we'll provide a sample cost calc comparing a per-AZ NLB vs centralized proxy pattern.
[09:38] Jordan: let's talk KV cache isolation again — suppose you want a shared cache across pods for the same customer to reduce cold starts, how do you do multi-AZ consistent cache without exposing other tenant data?
[09:52] Samira: we shard cache by customer-key and use ACLs. for higher isolation we can do dedicated Redis clusters or local in-memory per-node caches with warmup. the dedicated Redis option is simplest for strong tenant isolation at cost.
[10:10] Maya: what's the expected warmup time for a large 8k context window?
[10:18] Samira: depends on token locality — first long request touches a lot of KV slices; warm-up can be several hundred ms to a few seconds depending on model and batch. subsequent requests using cached prefixes are much faster. the bench will measure this explicitly.
[10:35] Evan: okay. last part — can you share a sample route table layout and the Security Group policy we should apply for restricted access?
[10:45] Samira: yes, we'll attach a sample: 1) endpoint ENIs allowed inbound from the app subnet SG on port 443; 2) NLB health check SG from health subnets; 3) management plane SG that allows Red-wood control plane CIDR for bootstrap. beware of overly broad 0.0.0.0/0 egress rules.
[11:05] Liam: for compliance we need to see KMS integration steps and proof of per-customer key usage — include that in the artifact pack.
[11:12] Jordan: will do.
[11:18] Samira: to recap next steps: we prepare the PrivateLink + NLB config doc, run the bench in your test VPC, send model artifact pull options, and share the security pack.
[11:30] Evan: good. let's schedule bench kickoff after we share VPC details. thanks everyone.
[11:40] Jordan: thanks all — I'll follow up with calendar invite and links.

Notes about transcript fidelity: occasional mis-transcriptions present, some product names slightly altered (PrivateLink spelled 'Private link' in a few lines), natural speech, interruptions and clarifications preserved.
